title: Field trip to GBA: Aerospace Sciences and Earth Informatics
description: This course aims to provide students with site visits in the Greater Bay Area (GBA). Through the guided visits to institutions and private sector relevant to the field of aerospace science and Earth informatics, students are given opportunity to explore and understand the current practices and research frontier in the field. Students are required to participate in all activities including the tutorial discussions and group presentation, and to submit an individual report afterwards.

title: Introduction to Aerospace Science and Earth Informatics
description: This introductory-level course offers a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts and applications within the fields of aerospace sciences and Earth informatics. Students will explore the evolution of the solar system, delve into the intricacies of Earth's planetary environment, understand the basics of the tools and technologies used to explore the Earth and space, and gain insights into the multidisciplinary field of aerospace science and engineering. The course emphasizes the acquisition and analysis of data from space and other planets, highlighting its significance in understanding our universe and improving life on Earth.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to:  Explain the processes involved in the formation and evolution of the solar system.  Describe the key components and dynamics of Earth's environment and compare them to other planetary environments.  Understand the basic tools and technologies used to explore space and Earth.  Understand the basic principles of aerospace science and engineering.  Apply data analysis techniques to interpret space and planetary data for various applications.  Recognize the significance of aerospace technologies in addressing global challenges and advancing scientific knowledge.
syllabus: Solar System Evolution:  Formation and development of the solar system  Characteristics of planets, moons, asteroids, and comets  The role of gravitational forces and cosmic events in shaping celestial bodies Earth and Planetary Environment:  Earth's atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere  Comparative study of planetary environments within the solar system  Impacts of space weather on planetary environments Aerospace Science:  Fundamental principles of flight and propulsion  Orbital and flight mechanics Overview of aerospace materials and structures Aerospace Engineering:  Design and development of aircraft and spacecraft  Systems engineering and integration in aerospace projects  Emerging technologies and innovations in aerospace engineering Applications of Space and Planetary Data:  Remote sensing and satellite imagery  Data analysis techniques for space and planetary exploration  Practical applications in climate science, natural disaster monitoring, and environmental management
recommended_readings: "An Introduction to the Solar System" by Neil McBride and Iain Gilmour for planetary evolution and environments"Foundations of astronomy" by Michael A. Seeds for solar system bodies"The Blue Planet: An Introduction to Earth System Science" by Brian Skinner and Barbara Murck"Introduction to Flight" by John D. Anderson Jr. for aerospace science“Spacecraft Systems Engineering" by Peter Fortescue et al. for aerospace Engineering"Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation" by Thomas M. Lillesand, Ralph W. Kiefer, and Jonathan W. Chipman for applications in space and planetary data

title: Rocket and Spacecraft Dynamics
requirements: Pre-requisite(s): ENGG1125 or MATH1010 or MATH1510 or MATH1520
description: This course introduces the fundamental dynamics of rockets and spacecraft. It focuses on how to design and analyze orbital trajectories and maneuvers using the two‑body problem. Students will also learn the basics of spacecraft attitude representation, attitude determination, and the related dynamics. The course emphasizes analytical methods, complemented by commonly used numerical techniques.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Apply and extend Newtonian mechanics for rockets, spacecraft, and orbital systems. Formulate and solve orbital mechanics problems, including the two‑body problem, orbital transfers, relative motion, and interplanetary trajectories. Evaluate and design spacecraft maneuvers and mission trajectories, such as Hohmann transfers, rendezvous operations, patched‑conic interplanetary paths, and gravity‑assist/free‑return trajectories. Model and assess spacecraft attitude dynamics and stability and apply control strategies. Analyze and optimize rocket vehicle performance, including thrust equations, staging, and landing. Integrate computational tools and simulation software to simulate, visualize, and validate spacecraft dynamics.
syllabus: Rocket & Flight Foundations:Rocket and space flight mechanicsRocket landing and vehicle dynamicsOrbital Mechanics:Two-body problemOrbital transfers, maneuvers and orbital analysisOrbital Environment & Trajectories:Ground tracks and relative motion in orbitGravity-assist and free-return trajectoriesSpacecraft Attitude:Attitude and rotational dynamicsEuler’s equations and linearizationStability analysisAttitude Control:Momentum management using thrusters, reaction wheels and control moment gyroscopeOrbital Simulation:Orbital simulation by programming and simulation software
required_readings: Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students by Howard D. Curtis
recommended_readings: “Fundamentals of Astrodynamics” by R. R. Bate et al.

title: Sensor Systems for Earth and Space Observation
description: Sensors are humanity’s primary interface with the Earth, space environment, and the universe. From observing the Earth’s surface and atmosphere, to measuring the near-Earth space environment, exploring planetary surfaces, and detecting extremely weak signals from deep space, sensor systems enable scientific discovery and engineering applications across aerospace and Earth informatics. This course introduces the principles, system-level design considerations, and applications of sensor systems used for Earth observation, space environment monitoring, planetary exploration, and astronomical observation. Emphasis is placed on understanding sensing concepts through real-world constraints, uncertainty, and design trade-offs. By examining sensors across different physical environments, students will develop an integrated and practical understanding of how sensing systems are designed, deployed, and interpreted in aerospace missions. The course is designed for upper-level undergraduate students and aims to bridge foundational science with mission-oriented thinking, preparing students for advanced studies and interdisciplinary applications in aerospace science and Earth informatics.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand the fundamental concepts and roles of sensor systems in Earth, space, and astronomical observation; Explain how different physical environments influence sensor design, performance, and limitations; Interpret sensor data with awareness of uncertainty, noise, and measurement constraints; Compare and evaluate sensor options based on mission objectives and system-level trade-offs; Apply system-level thinking to propose sensor configurations for Earth observation and space missions.

title: Aerospace Earth Informatics
requirements: Pre-requisite(s): ENGG1125 or MATH1010 or MATH1510 or MATH1520
description: Exploring how aerospace platforms collect, transmit, and transform space data. Students learn the full pipeline of Earth Informatics as applied to aerospace missions: sensing, data assimilation, interpretation, analysis, transformation, and classification by machine learning with artificial intelligence. The course includes space mission datasets and teaches students to apply Earth‑observation data in the context of the Earth environments.
